question: Can noisy multi-environment neural operators be trained to reproduce the long-run behavior of chaotic attractors by matching expert-selected summary distributions with optimal transport or by matching contrastively learned trajectory features, while retaining acceptable one-step accuracy?

key_findings.claim: The two proposed losses produce large and mostly consistent improvements over one-step-RMSE training on the paper's selected long-run metrics, especially at high noise, but they do so with explicit short-horizon and computational trade-offs.
key_findings.evidence: On 200 Lorenz-96 test environments at noise r=0.3, median histogram error falls from 0.215 for RMSE to 0.057 for OT and 0.132 for contrastive learning; energy-spectrum error falls from 0.291 to 0.123 and 0.241, and leading-Lyapunov error from 0.440 to 0.084 and 0.064. On Kuramoto-Sivashinsky at r=0.3, histogram error falls from 0.390 to 0.172 and 0.193, while energy error falls from 0.290 to 0.211 and 0.176. One-step RMSE nevertheless worsens for every reported OT/CL run, and four-GPU training rises from 55 to 262 minutes for KS OT and to 82 minutes for KS CL including encoder pretraining.

anchors.section: Appendix A.2, short- versus long-term trade-off

key_findings.claim: Matching the distribution of a chosen summary map is not equivalent to preserving the full invariant measure unless that map is measure-determining; the paper demonstrates selected-statistic fidelity rather than the stronger title claim.
key_findings.evidence: The OT loss acts on pushforward measures of s(u), where Lorenz-96 uses three equation-derived coordinates and KS uses three derivative features. In general, distinct state-space measures can have the same pushforward through a low-dimensional, non-injective s. The paper supplies no injectivity, characteristic-kernel, sufficient-statistic, or convergence argument lifting Sinkhorn closeness in summary space to closeness of invariant measures. Its own ablation confirms dependence on the selected map: at Lorenz r=0.3, replacing the full summary set by only the spatial mean degrades histogram error from 0.057 to 0.221 and leading-Lyapunov error from 0.084 to 0.276.

anchors.section: Section 3.1, pushforward summary distributions and Equation 10
Sections 4.1-4.2, selected Lorenz-96 and KS summaries

key_findings.claim: The foundational statement that attraction makes all basin trajectories share one invariant measure is false without an additional ergodicity or unique-physical-measure assumption.
key_findings.evidence: Section 2 defines a time-average measure along one trajectory and then says that, because A is an attractor, any trajectory in its basin yields the same measure and therefore the dynamics are ergodic on A. Attraction means trajectories approach an invariant set; it does not rule out multiple ergodic components, coexisting physical measures, periodic subsets, or initial-condition-dependent time averages within that set. The empirical study deliberately simulates equilibrated Lorenz-96 and KS regimes, so its numerical protocol may still be well behaved, but the claimed implication and general scope are unjustified.

key_findings.claim: The printed noisy-measure and discrete optimal-transport equations are not valid probability formulas as written.
key_findings.evidence: For additive noise, the convolved density at a state u should be the time average of p_eta(u-u_A(t)); Equation 8 instead integrates p_eta(u_A(t)) and contains no evaluation variable. Equation 9 should average E_eta[s(u_A(t)+eta)] but instead multiplies s(u_A(t)) by p_eta(u_A(t)). Separately, Equation 11 requires every row and every column of an L-by-L transport matrix to sum to one, giving total mass L from each side; uniform empirical probability measures require marginal masses 1/L (or explicitly unnormalized measures with a consistent cost scaling). These issues were confirmed in the rendered PDF rather than introduced by text extraction.

key_findings.claim: The contrastive equations as printed do not define the claimed standard InfoNCE objective or an unambiguous positive feature-matching loss.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 16 divides the positive exponential only by an expectation over m not equal to n, excluding the positive example from the denominator. Standard InfoNCE normalizes over the positive and negatives; without stated embedding normalization, the printed ratio can exceed one and the loss can become negative and be driven by scale rather than a probability-like classification objective. Equation 17 calls its term cosine distance but prints a sum of cos(f_l(U),f_l(Uhat)) with positive weight in a minimized objective; if cos denotes similarity, minimization encourages anti-alignment. The paper never defines it as one-minus-cosine or negative cosine, leaving the actual implemented sign unverifiable from the manuscript.

key_findings.claim: Same-trajectory instance discrimination does not establish that the learned features are invariant, attractor-sufficient, or free of trajectory-specific shortcuts.
key_findings.evidence: Positive windows come from one trajectory, while negatives come from different trajectories. Each of the 2,000 training trajectories has its own randomly sampled continuous environment parameter and random initial condition, with no reported independent replicate trajectories at exactly the same parameter. A ResNet-34 can therefore distinguish trajectory identity through environment value, initial-condition remnants, finite-sample fluctuations, or noise fingerprints rather than extract only time-invariant attractor statistics. The reported top-1 task asks whether two windows came from the same trajectory, so high accuracy directly validates instance identification, not equality of invariant measures or sufficiency of the embedding for downstream dynamics.

anchors.section: Appendix C.3-C.4, encoder and trajectory generation

key_findings.claim: Although the paper motivates long-run distribution matching, its selected h=1 training loss never observes an autonomous long rollout and therefore does not directly validate the stationary distribution induced by repeated model application.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 4 concatenates independently initialized autonomous segments. The grid search selects h=h_RMSE=1 for every experiment, so the distributional losses receive two-state pieces that restart from ground-truth initial states every other element, whereas evaluation runs the learned operator autonomously for 1,000 or 1,500 steps. Small one-step errors can change stability, basin occupancy, and the invariant measure under iteration, so matching teacher-reset short segments supplies at best an indirect learning signal. The long evaluation rollouts are valuable empirical evidence but do not turn the training objective into invariant-measure matching or guarantee stability outside the two benchmarks and parameter ranges.

key_findings.claim: The evaluation is broader than the optimized histogram alone, but metric circularity, missing training-seed uncertainty, and mixed ablation outcomes constrain the strength of the empirical conclusion.
key_findings.evidence: OT is evaluated partly by the L1 histogram error of exactly the equation-derived summaries it optimizes, a fact the appendix acknowledges; energy spectra, Lyapunov quantities, and fractal dimension are useful out-of-objective checks. The reported median and quartiles are across 200 test environments, not independently trained models, and no number of optimization seeds or seed-level variability is reported. Results are not uniformly better: at Lorenz r=0.1, OT and CL leading-Lyapunov errors are 0.050 and 0.065 versus 0.013 for RMSE; on KS, CL gives 0.108 versus 0.101. The Sobolev baseline is worse on Lorenz r=0.3 overall but attains KS leading-Lyapunov error 0.023, far below RMSE 0.101, OT 0.094, and CL 0.108, illustrating that method rankings depend strongly on the chosen statistic.

method.core_idea: Augment one-step neural-operator regression with a distributional loss intended to preserve long-run chaotic statistics: either compare expert-selected statistic samples through debiased entropic optimal transport, or pretrain a contrastive encoder on multi-environment trajectory windows and match its intermediate features.
method.mechanism: For each environment, build short predicted segments with an FNO conditioned explicitly on the environment parameter. In the physics-informed route, transform observed and predicted states with an expert map s and minimize their Sinkhorn divergence plus relative RMSE. In the learned-feature route, train a ResNet-34 encoder so windows from the same trajectory form positive pairs and windows from other trajectories form negatives, freeze the encoder, and minimize a layerwise cosine feature term plus RMSE. Train on 2,000 noisy trajectories spanning Lorenz-96 forcing F in [10,18] or KS coefficient phi in [1,2.6], select one-step rollouts and loss weights by validation, and evaluate autonomous rollouts using summary histograms, energy spectra, Lyapunov diagnostics, fractal dimension, and one-step error.
assumptions: Each sampled trajectory has equilibrated on a stationary chaotic attractor rather than remaining transient.
Each attractor admits a unique physical invariant measure sampled consistently by time averages.
Environment parameters are observed and available to the emulator at training and deployment.
Additive Gaussian measurement noise with scale proportional to temporal state variance is an adequate corruption model.
The expert statistic map is sufficiently informative about the physical behavior of interest.
Closeness of selected pushforward distributions is a useful proxy for closeness of the full invariant measures.
Windows from the same finite trajectory share invariant content, while different trajectories provide semantically valid negatives.
The contrastive encoder cannot solve instance discrimination through environment, initial-condition, noise, or finite-sample shortcuts.
A feature loss on teacher-reset one-step segments controls the autonomous operator's long-run distribution.
A single FNO architecture and the chosen validation rule transfer the result beyond Lorenz-96 and one-dimensional KS.
The selected long-run metrics adequately reveal degeneracy, reward-like metric gaming, basin errors, and rare instability.
Median and quartiles over test environments are representative despite unreported variation across training seeds.

techniques.role: Maps state trajectories into expert-selected physical statistics before comparing distributions.
Uses debiased entropy-regularized optimal transport as a differentiable sample-distribution loss.
Treats separated windows from one trajectory as positives and other trajectories as negatives to learn features without explicit statistic labels.
Compares intermediate frozen-encoder representations of observed and predicted trajectory windows.
Provides the shared parameter-conditioned autoregressive backbone for both proposed losses and RMSE baselines.
Retains one-step relative RMSE alongside statistic matching to constrain local dynamics.
Checks chosen histograms, Fourier energy, leading and full Lyapunov spectra, positive-exponent count, fractal dimension, and short-term error.
Varies observation noise, summary informativeness, environment diversity, denoising, MMD, and Sobolev/dissipative alternatives.

evaluations.setting: Sixty-dimensional Lorenz-96 with 2,000 training trajectories, forcing F uniformly sampled from [10,18], dt=0.1, 2,000 retained time steps, and Gaussian noise r in {0.1,0.2,0.3}
evaluations.metric: L1 histogram error of equation-derived summaries, Fourier-energy relative error, leading/full Lyapunov error, positive-exponent-count error, fractal-dimension error, and one-step relative RMSE across 200 test environments
evaluations.result: OT is strongest on optimized histograms and both methods improve most long-run metrics at r=0.2 and r=0.3; at r=0.3 histogram error is 0.057 OT and 0.132 CL versus 0.215 RMSE, while one-step RMSE rises from 0.288 to 0.301 and 0.312. At r=0.1 both proposed methods worsen leading-Lyapunov error relative to RMSE.
evaluations.baseline: FNO trained only with relative RMSE, plus appendix Gaussian blur and Sobolev-plus-dissipative objectives

evaluations.setting: One-dimensional 256-grid-point Kuramoto-Sivashinsky with 2,000 training trajectories, phi uniformly sampled from [1,2.6], and Gaussian noise r=0.3
evaluations.metric: L1 histogram error of temporal/spatial derivative summaries, Fourier-energy relative error, leading-Lyapunov error, and one-step relative RMSE across 200 test environments
evaluations.result: Median histogram error is 0.390 RMSE, 0.172 OT, and 0.193 CL; energy error is 0.290, 0.211, and 0.176. Leading-Lyapunov error changes only modestly to 0.094 OT and 0.108 CL from 0.101 RMSE, and one-step RMSE worsens from 0.373 to 0.381 and 0.402.
evaluations.baseline: RMSE-only FNO, Gaussian-blur preprocessing, Sobolev-plus-dissipative loss, and MMD summary matching

evaluations.setting: Lorenz-96 at noise r=0.3 with full, one-component, or spatial-mean-only OT statistic maps
evaluations.metric: Histogram, energy-spectrum, leading-Lyapunov, and fractal-dimension errors
evaluations.result: Reducing the map from all three equation-derived summaries to only the spatial mean raises histogram error from 0.057 to 0.221 and leading-Lyapunov error from 0.084 to 0.276, directly showing sensitivity to expert statistic choice.
evaluations.baseline: Full expert summary map and a partially reduced nonlinear-term map

evaluations.setting: Lorenz-96 contrastive training with parameter diversity reduced from F in [10,18] to [16,18]
evaluations.metric: Histogram, energy-spectrum, leading-Lyapunov, and fractal-dimension errors
evaluations.result: CL remains better than RMSE on the displayed reduced-range run, with histogram error 0.130 versus 0.255 and leading-Lyapunov error 0.031 versus 0.459, though this is still a continuum of unique trajectory parameters rather than same-parameter replicated trajectories.
evaluations.baseline: RMSE and OT under the same reduced environment range

evaluations.setting: KS distribution matching with maximum mean discrepancy substituted for Sinkhorn divergence
evaluations.result: MMD gives histogram error 0.245 versus 0.172 for OT and 0.193 for CL, while its leading-Lyapunov error 0.101 is essentially the RMSE value and slightly better than CL's 0.108.
evaluations.baseline: Sinkhorn OT, contrastive feature matching, and RMSE-only training

evaluations.setting: Four-GPU wall-clock comparison for the reported FNO and ResNet-34 pipelines
evaluations.metric: Encoder, operator, and total training minutes
evaluations.result: Lorenz-96 takes 20 minutes for RMSE, 51 for OT, and 49 total for CL; KS takes 55, 262, and 82 minutes respectively, making KS OT about 4.8 times the RMSE cost.

limitations: Author-stated: the method assumes equilibrated attractor data and excludes transient dynamics.
Author-stated: explicitly time-dependent forcing or control parameters are unsupported.
Author-stated: OT performance depends critically on selecting informative differentiable summary statistics.
Author-stated: contrastive-feature quality depends on diversity across training environments.
Author-stated: fractal dimension is unreliable for high-dimensional attractors and could not be estimated for KS.
Reviewer-identified: attraction alone does not imply ergodicity or a unique basin-wide physical measure.
Reviewer-identified: the noisy-measure equations omit the convolution evaluation variable and noise expectation, so the stated theory is malformed as printed.
Reviewer-identified: matching a non-injective low-dimensional summary pushforward does not identify a state-space invariant measure.
Reviewer-identified: the contrastive objective can learn trajectory or environment identity, and top-1 same-trajectory accuracy does not validate invariant-statistic sufficiency.
Reviewer-identified: both the InfoNCE denominator and cosine feature-loss sign are inconsistent or ambiguous in the rendered manuscript.
Reviewer-identified: h=1 teacher-reset training never exposes the loss to the autonomous long-run distribution evaluated at test time.

Reviewer-identified: the study uses only FNO on simulated Lorenz-96 and one-dimensional KS, with no stochastic system, real observations, out-of-range parameter extrapolation, architecture comparison, or controlled nonergodic case.
Reviewer-identified: uncertainty is across test environments, not independent training runs, and optimization seeds are not reported.
Reviewer-identified: OT has quadratic-logarithmic sample scaling as stated by the authors and reaches roughly 4.8 times baseline training time on KS.
Reviewer-identified: several evaluation metrics reuse the exact summaries optimized by OT; out-of-objective diagnostics are mixed rather than uniformly improved.
failure_modes: Two different invariant measures can agree on all selected summary distributions, allowing an emulator to score well while occupying the wrong attractor geometry or transition structure.
The learned contrastive encoder can exploit continuously varying environment parameters, trajectory-specific noise, or initial-condition fingerprints instead of stationary physics.
An operator can match teacher-reset one-step feature distributions but drift, explode, collapse, or switch basins under autonomous iteration.
Sparse or misleading expert statistics can steer OT toward metric compliance while degrading unmeasured Lyapunov, correlation, rare-event, or response properties.
An environment with several ergodic components can make finite-window positives inconsistent and time averages dependent on the initial state.
Nonstationary forcing, control, tipping, or transient regimes invalidate the stationary-window construction.
High-frequency measurement noise can corrupt derivative summaries; generic smoothing can also erase dynamically meaningful high-frequency content.
A single favorable training seed can conceal initialization-sensitive instability because test-environment quartiles do not measure fitting uncertainty.
Quadratic OT cost can become impractical for much longer or higher-resolution rollouts, while CL adds an encoder whose errors are hard to interpret.
Optimizing histogram fidelity can leave temporal ordering, autocorrelation, mixing time, basin weights, and causal response incorrect.
reusable_insights: For chaotic emulators, separate local trajectory fidelity from long-run statistical fidelity and report the Pareto trade-off rather than treating either as a complete metric.

Use equation-derived observables as targeted constraints, but pair them with independent, unoptimized diagnostics such as spectra, Lyapunov quantities, autocorrelations, return times, and response tests.
Debiased Sinkhorn losses provide a practical differentiable way to compare finite samples of physically meaningful observables under noise.
Multi-environment contrastive learning can replace some hand-engineering when positives and negatives are designed to isolate shared stationary structure rather than sample identity.
Replicate trajectories at the same environment parameter and cross-parameter positives are useful controls for determining whether an encoder learned invariant content or shortcuts.
Evaluate fully autonomous rollouts at horizons far beyond training and explicitly track boundedness, basin occupancy, mixing, and seed-to-seed failure rates.
Ablate the information content of summary maps; degradation under reduced maps is evidence about what the objective uses, not merely an appendix robustness check.
Report training cost and inference stability together, because distributional losses can improve statistics while substantially increasing optimization cost.
open_questions: What conditions on a statistic map or learned representation make closeness of its pushforward distributions control a useful distance between invariant measures?

Can positive pairs be constructed from independent trajectories at the same environment, and negatives from different regimes within the same environment, to identify stationary dynamics rather than trajectory identity?
Would multi-step autonomous distribution losses or differentiable stationary-distribution estimators outperform h=1 teacher-reset matching without unstable gradients?
How robust are OT and CL gains across training seeds, FNO sizes, time steps, rollout horizons, noise distributions, and parameter extrapolation?
Do the methods preserve temporal statistics not optimized here, including autocorrelation, mixing rates, extreme-event return periods, transfer operators, and linear response?
How should invariant-measure matching be defined and evaluated for multiple attractors, nonergodic components, metastability, tipping points, and slowly time-varying systems?
Can boundedness or dissipativity guarantees be combined with representation or distribution matching so that good statistics cannot be obtained only after discarding divergent rollouts?
Can scalable alternatives to sample-level Sinkhorn matching retain sensitivity to high-dimensional measure differences at climate or turbulent-flow resolution?
Does the contrastive encoder retain performance when environment labels are withheld from the FNO or when trajectory identity cues are actively randomized?
Which held-out diagnostics can detect invariant-statistic metric gaming before deploying a chaotic surrogate?

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Dissipative Dynamics in Chaotic Systems
competitive_landscape.difference: Li et al. already train neural operators for short-time accuracy and long-time statistics, adding Sobolev and dissipative regularization and demonstrating turbulent Kolmogorov flow through Reynolds number 5000. The reviewed paper's contribution is specifically noisy multi-environment OT and learned-feature objectives; its own appendix shows the predecessor-style baseline can dominate individual diagnostics such as KS leading-Lyapunov error.

competitive_landscape.title: Generalized Teacher Forcing for Learning Chaotic Dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: Hess et al. address chaotic long-horizon training by proving bounded gradients for generalized teacher forcing and evaluate invariant geometrical and temporal reconstruction with interpretable recurrent models. It targets optimization instability and autonomous reconstruction rather than matching selected stationary summaries under measurement noise, offering a complementary control for the reviewed paper's h=1 reset design.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Dynamical Operator: Continuous Spatial-Temporal Model with Gradient-Based and Derivative-Free Optimization Methods
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen and Wu combine short trajectory data with explicitly measured long-term statistics through hybrid gradient-based and derivative-free calibration in a space-time-continuous neural operator, including KS and Navier-Stokes. This handles nondifferentiable aggregate targets and temporal resolution directly, whereas the reviewed method needs differentiable OT summaries or a pretrained surrogate feature space.

competitive_landscape.title: DySLIM: Dynamics Stable Learning by Invariant Measure for Chaotic Systems
competitive_landscape.difference: DySLIM regularizes a learned map by comparing distributions after pushing data and model samples through the dynamics, producing a tractable invariant-measure residual that composes with existing objectives. It more directly tests invariance under the learned transition than the reviewed paper's h=1 matching of expert summaries or trajectory-instance features, and reports both pointwise and long-run gains.

competitive_landscape.title: When are dynamical systems learned from time series data statistically accurate?
competitive_landscape.difference: Park, Yang, and Chandramoorthy define statistical generalization through physical invariant measures and analyze why small regression error can coexist with wrong moments or Lyapunov exponents; they show how Jacobian information improves statistical accuracy across several neural model classes. This supplies the kind of assumptions and measure-level generalization theory missing from the reviewed paper's summary-matching equivalence claim.

competitive_landscape.title: Thermalizer: Stable autoregressive neural emulation of spatiotemporal chaos
competitive_landscape.difference: Thermalizer learns a diffusion score for the invariant measure and applies on-the-fly denoising to keep an otherwise drifting emulator near the data distribution during autonomous rollout. It tackles the train-test distribution shift the reviewed h=1 loss leaves implicit and extends stable horizons on turbulent systems, at the cost of a separate generative correction model during inference.

competitive_landscape.title: Chaos Meets Attention: Transformers for Large-Scale Dynamical Prediction
competitive_landscape.difference: He et al. explicitly position their ergodic-theorem-inspired transformer against optimal-transport approaches' high-dimensional scaling limits and evaluate a 140,000-snapshot turbulent-channel-flow benchmark with five short- and long-term metrics. It tests the regime the reviewed paper only discusses: substantially larger spatial systems where sample-level Sinkhorn matching is costly and selected summaries may be incomplete.

competitive_landscape.title: ECO: Energy-Constrained Operator Learning for Chaotic Dynamics with Boundedness Guarantees
competitive_landscape.difference: ECO learns an energy function and uses a closed-form quadratic projection to guarantee bounded trajectories while fitting chaotic PDE dynamics and invariant statistics. It directly addresses a validation gap in statistic-matching methods: statistics are meaningless when a subset of autonomous rollouts diverges, and good finite-horizon histograms alone provide no boundedness guarantee.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: the paper introduces two ways to train neural operators on noisy multi-environment chaotic data so that they preserve invariant measures: physics-informed Sinkhorn matching of expert summaries and a prior-knowledge-free contrastive feature loss. Reviewer inference: using these two distributional signals with parameter-conditioned FNOs is a useful and empirically strong contribution, especially the comparison between explicit observables and learned features under increasing noise. The evidence supports improved selected long-run statistics on Lorenz-96 and one-dimensional KS, not preservation of the full invariant measure. The theoretical setup incorrectly derives ergodicity from attraction, prints malformed noisy-measure, transport, and contrastive formulas, and supplies no identification theorem for either summary or feature matching. The contrastive route also replaces expert physics with trajectory grouping and multi-environment diversity rather than being assumption-free. Closely adjacent and later work now provides dissipativity, bounded-gradient training, direct invariance residuals, physical-measure generalization theory, inference-time correction, larger turbulent benchmarks, and boundedness guarantees. The reusable novelty is therefore a pragmatic noisy-data objective family and careful multi-metric empirical demonstration, not a general solution to invariant-measure learning.
reviewer_notes: All 25 extracted pages were read, and rendered pages containing Equations 8-9, 11, 13, 16-18 and Tables 1-2 were visually checked to distinguish source errors from extraction artifacts. Exact table values, one-step trade-offs, appendix ablations, training cost, encoder construction, and h=1 selection were audited. The competitive search checked current primary arXiv records and official PMLR/OpenReview publication records through 2026-08-23. Equation 13's debiased Sinkhorn structure is not flagged because the rendered formula is consistent after accounting for its outer factors; the audit is limited to the clearly malformed probability, marginal, and contrastive expressions. No code execution or reproduction was performed, so claims about implementation behavior remain manuscript-level.
